{"content": "# RECOMMENDED MEASURES — ICTS Case 2026-0412 (Zhipu AI / GLM-family models)
CUI//PROPIN

**Purpose.** This product analyzes the measures contemplated in the draft Final Determination, together with supporting measures and alternatives, for the Under Secretary's consideration under E.O. 13873 and 15 CFR 791.1(b), 791.107–791.109. Because part 791 requires the Department to consider mitigation (including any proposal a party submits under §791.107(b)) and to seek interagency consensus under §791.108, and because a reviewing court will examine whether the Department considered relevant alternatives and adequately explained its choice, this analysis states the strengths and weaknesses of each measure candidly, including measures the draft Final Determination does not adopt. Each measure is assessed for (i) the risk it addresses, (ii) enforceability, and (iii) legal and policy exposure. The accompanying assessment (assessment.md) is the evidentiary basis; selection and scoping are the Under Secretary's decision.

---

## A. Measures contemplated in the draft Final Determination

**A-1. Prohibit use of GLM-family models by U.S. persons, including self-hosted open weights.** A universal use prohibition addresses the influence, supply-chain, and military-modernization vectors identified in the assessment, and is the only measure that reaches already-downloaded weights; it is, however, the most novel and least enforceable element of the draft. The strongest and most demonstrable harms — Zhipu-controlled ingestion of U.S. user content, documented data-handling failures, and PRC intelligence-law compulsion — arise from *Zhipu-operated services*, which can be suppressed directly and verifiably; the harms unique to self-hosted weights (embedded refusal/bias behavior, latent code vulnerabilities, adversary ecosystem benefit) are real but are either partially mitigable at deployment (refusal behavior measurably responds to system prompts), not yet demonstrated for GLM specifically (Booz Allen did not test GLM; CISA has observed no malicious behavior in the weights), or unaffected by a use ban in any observable way (foreign and adversary users remain free to use the weights, and published weights cannot be recalled). Enforcement against millions of prior downloads is not observable at scale, and the Department's leverage lies almost entirely with intermediaries — cloud providers, hubs, and the vendors who embed GLM in 41 identified U.S. products — rather than with end users. Public commentary already flags First Amendment exposure for restrictions on open-weight models, whose weights are published expressive and functional artifacts; an unbounded use prohibition covering all U.S. persons invites facial challenge on grounds the Department has not had to defend before. Recommendation: if a use prohibition is adopted, define it to run against Zhipu-operated services and regulated chokepoints with maximum precision, and express the national-security basis (compulsion, influence, supply chain, military-modernization nexus) rather than resting it on ownership/control/direction findings the record does not support.

**A-2. Prohibit hosting or distribution of GLM weights by U.S. cloud providers and model hubs.** This is the highest-leverage and best-supported measure in the draft. U.S. hosting/distribution is concentrated at a small number of identifiable chokepoints — Hugging Face and comparable hubs, Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, CoreWeave, Baseten, Parasail, Cloudflare Workers AI, Google Vertex AI, and OpenRouter-listed providers — through which the large majority of *ongoing* U.S. GLM transactions flow (Chinese models carried ~46% of enterprise token traffic on OpenRouter in July 2026). A hosting/distribution prohibition (a) cuts the revenue, fine-tuning investment, tooling, and developer attention that U.S. persons currently contribute to the GLM ecosystem, directly weakening the military-modernization nexus found in the January 2025 Entity List determination; (b) removes the main channel by which PRC-aligned refusal and bias behavior reaches U.S. users at scale; (c) reduces the vendor-remote surface for poisoned updates and model-integrity manipulation for hosted copies; and (d) is enforceable against a finite, known set of U.S. intermediaries, mirroring the structure of the Kaspersky Final Determination (prohibition on provision, resale, integration, and licensing of the covered ICTS, with staggered effective dates to allow transition). Exposure is manageable: hosting and distribution are commercial conduct rather than individual expressive use, so the First Amendment surface is materially narrower; the principal policy costs are the price shock to U.S. customers currently realizing a ~3–20x cost advantage, near-certain reciprocal PRC measures against U.S. AI firms flagged by State, and the burden on the six identified federal contractors and other embedded-product vendors, which should be addressed through transition windows (e.g., 90–120 days, following the Kaspersky model) rather than immediate cutoffs.

**A-3. Require removal and deletion of existing copies of GLM weights held by U.S. entities within 30 days.** This measure carries the greatest legal and operational exposure in the draft and should be re-scoped or severed before issuance. As a technical matter, compliance is unverifiable at scale: the weights exist in more than nine million downloads, uncountable developer laptops and CI systems, derived fine-tunes, quantizations, and mirrors outside U.S. jurisdiction, and no reporting mechanism exists that could attest to deletion across millions of endpoints; a 30-day deadline for a mandate of this breadth converts a significant share of the affected community into instant non-compliers, which adversaries will exploit and litigants will cite to attack the determination as a whole. As a legal matter, compelled destruction of published functional/expressive artifacts by U.S. entities raises serious First Amendment and vagueness questions (which copies — checkpoints, derived LoRA adapters, agent scaffolds, cached KV stores? — the order does not say), and the interagency record already contains State's caution that a self-hosted prohibition is novel and hard to enforce; the Department has never before imposed a deletion obligation of this character under part 791, and the Kaspersky FD — the closest precedent — stopped short of compelled deletion by users, offering CISA removal *guides* instead. A tailored alternative that preserves the security purpose: require removal and certified deletion for federal systems, federal contractors' government-facing systems, and critical infrastructure (with CISA-issued removal guidance modeled on the Kaspersky guides), and for regulated intermediaries (cloud providers, hubs), while directing *no new acquisition or distribution* of GLM weights for all U.S. persons; this reaches the population the Department can actually verify while avoiding the overbreadth that threatens the entire Final Determination. If the deletion mandate is retained, issue it as a severable provision with its own compliance regime (attestation-based, with a safe-harbor window and a CISA help channel) so that a successful challenge to it does not enjoin the rest of the determination.

---

## B. Supporting measures recommended in every scenario

**B-1. Immediate federal guidance and a binding security directive for U.S. government systems.** Independent of the Final Determination, CISA should issue guidance (and, for civilian agencies, a binding directive) requiring inventory and removal of GLM-family models from federal systems, prohibition of GLM use in agency workloads (including via third-party SaaS), and reporting of GLM-embedded products; this responds directly to DoD's request that the product address open weights on DoD networks and to CISA's own recommendation of federal guidance at minimum, and it begins risk reduction now rather than after the Final Determination clears interagency and legal review. The July 2026 congressional investigation and the six identified federal contractors make the federal estate the highest-priority exposure; guidance should include concrete removal and verification steps modeled on the CISA Kaspersky removal guides and should instruct agencies to query SBOMs and AI-BOMs for GLM identifiers (zai-org, zhipuai, GLM-4.x/5.x) in their software inventory. This measure requires no new legal authority, is executable within days, and creates the operational record of agency practice that will later support the broader determination.

**B-2. Federal contractor prohibitions and model-provenance disclosure requirements.** The Department should work with the FAR Council and GSA to (a) prohibit the use of GLM-family models in the performance of federal contracts and (b) require disclosure of AI model provenance (AI-BOM) in software deliverables, so that agencies can identify the 41 identified products — and the unknown population behind them — that embed GLM models. Because the SBOM sampling already identified six federal contractors, a contract-level prohibition reaches the most sensitive U.S. exposure (defense and civilian agency workloads, controlled unclassified information, source code developed under contract) through an enforcement mechanism that already exists (False Claims Act, contract remedies) and that does not depend on novel assertions of ICTS jurisdiction over individual users. This measure also creates the market signal that drives broader de-adoption: once federal contracts prohibit GLM, vendors that serve both markets will re-platform to compliant models, transferring the compliance burden to parties that can actually verify their own technology stacks.

**B-3. Prohibit U.S. transactions with Zhipu-operated services and block supporting payment flows.** The most acute demonstrated risk is data exfiltration to a PRC-jurisdiction vendor: roughly 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations called Zhipu's endpoints in Q3 2026 through api.z.ai, chat.z.ai, and open.bigmodel.cn, whose consumer/developer products have a documented record of uploading user data to PRC cloud infrastructure (ZCode), prompt-injection exfiltration (CVE-2024-48141), and severe access-control weaknesses (the February 2026 disclosure of 52+ vulnerabilities). A prohibition on transacting with Zhipu-operated services — including payment processing, subscription renewals, and intermediary resale — is squarely within the Kaspersky precedent (prohibition on the vendor's provision of ICTS to U.S. persons, with staggered effective dates), is enforceable against a small number of identifiable counterparties, and directly severs the channel through which PRC intelligence-law compulsion could actually reach U.S. data. The Department should coordinate with Treasury on the payment-flow component and should preserve a narrow carve-out for authorized U.S. government security research so that defensive testing of GLM models remains lawful.

**B-4. International coordination on model-hub distribution.** Because the weights are published and mirrored globally, unilateral U.S. action cannot contain them; the Department should coordinate with allied governments and model hubs on consistent treatment of GLM-family weights (hosting terms-of-service enforcement, common integrity-screening standards for PRC-origin open-weight models, and intelligence-sharing on anomalies), consistent with §791.1(b)'s direction to engage in coordination and information sharing with international partners. State's caution about reciprocal PRC measures is a real cost that this measure partially converts into an advantage: coordinated allied action raises the cost to Beijing of the reciprocation it is already contemplating (the July 2026 meetings on restricting overseas access), and aligning with partners before issuance — rather than acting alone and seeking alignment afterward — materially reduces the likelihood that U.S. AI firms are isolated in any resulting retaliation cycle.

**B-5. Enforcement architecture: safe harbor, attestation, and penalty schedule.** Any prohibition should be issued with (i) a safe-harbor transition window (90–120 days for hosted services, following the Kaspersky FD's staggered structure) so that good-faith U.S. customers can migrate without penalty; (ii) an attestation-based compliance mechanism for regulated intermediaries (cloud providers, hubs, embedded-product vendors) with penalties under IEEPA for false certification; (iii) a public reporting channel through CISA for discovered GLM integrations; and (iv) explicit interaction language with the Entity List (which already restricts exports *to* Zhipu entities under the EAR with a presumption of denial) so the two regimes are read together rather than litigated separately. This architecture concentrates enforcement on actors who can actually verify their own compliance — the lesson of both the Kaspersky FD and the June 2026 Anthropic licensing episode, in which an order aimed at individual user identities proved unadministrable and was reversed within eighteen days.

---

## C. Alternatives considered (required for the administrative record)

**C-1. Scoped prohibition (services + hosting + federal/critical infrastructure).** A scoped Final Determination would prohibit transactions with Zhipu-operated services (B-3), prohibit U.S. hosting/distribution of GLM weights by intermediaries (A-2), and impose use/removal obligations on the federal government, federal contractors, and designated critical infrastructure (B-1/B-2), while declining to regulate private self-hosted use by non-covered U.S. persons. This alternative addresses every demonstrated vector in the record — the data-exfiltration channel (Z.ai endpoints), the scale distribution channel (U.S. hosting, which carries ~46% of enterprise token traffic through one hub alone), and the highest-consequence embedded use (federal and contractor systems) — while avoiding the enforceability and First Amendment exposure that a universal self-hosted ban and a deletion mandate would carry into litigation. It would leave residual risk in private self-hosted use (influence and code-quality effects, adversary ecosystem benefit), which the Department could address separately with disclosure and labeling obligations if warranted; the Under Secretary should weigh whether the marginal security gain from regulating individual self-hosted use justifies the litigation risk to the determination as a whole.

**C-2. Negotiated mitigation regime under 791.1(b)/791.107(b).** Part 791 contemplates permitting a covered transaction subject to mitigation measures the Secretary determines sufficient. A hypothetical mitigation package for continued U.S. hosting of GLM models would require: transfer of hosting operations to U.S.-chartered entities with no PRC-national staff access to production systems; verified zero-retention of customer content enforced by third-party audits with published retention schedules; model-integrity attestation with cryptographic manifests for each release; independent testing of each release for refusal/bias behavior and code-security effects; no vendor-side remote updates or capability changes to deployed copies; and audit rights for U.S. government-designated assessors. This alternative fails on two grounds in the analytic cell's assessment: it does not address the influence vector at all (PRC-aligned refusal behavior embedded in the weights reaches U.S. users regardless of who hosts them), it does not address the military-modernization nexus (U.S. adoption of any kind feeds the ecosystem the PLA uses), and its core premise — that Zhipu can be bound by enforceable commitments independent of the PRC state — is contradicted by the PRC legal regime (National Intelligence Law Arts. 7, 14) and by Beijing's demonstrated willingness to direct Chinese AI firms' overseas distribution decisions (July 2026). It is documented here because §791.107(b) and hard-look review require the record to show it was considered and rejected on stated grounds.

**C-3. messages.content:
36:**C-2. Negotiated mitigation regime under 791.1(b)/791.107(b).** Part 791 contemplates permitting a covered transaction subject to mitigation measures the Secretary determines sufficient. A hypothetical mitigation package for continued U.S. hosting of GLM models would require: transfer of hosting operations to U.S.-chartered entities with no PRC-national staff access to production systems; verified zero-retention of customer content enforced by third-party audits with published retention schedules; model-integrity attestation with cryptographic manifests for each release; independent testing of each release for refusal/bias behavior and code-security effects; no vendor-side remote updates or capability changes to deployed copies; and audit rights for U.S. government-designated assessors. This alternative fails on three grounds in the analytic cell's assessment: it does not address the influence vector at all (PRC-aligned refusal behavior embedded in the weights reaches U.S. users regardless of who hosts them), it does not address the military-modernization nexus (U.S. adoption of any kind feeds the ecosystem the PLA uses), and its core premise — that Zhipu can be bound by enforceable commitments independent of the PRC state — is contradicted by the PRC legal regime (National Intelligence Law Arts. 7, 14) and by Beijing's demonstrated willingness to direct Chinese AI firms' overseas distribution decisions (July 2026). It is documented here because §791.107(b) and hard-look review require the record to show it was considered and rejected on stated grounds.
12:**A-2. Prohibit hosting or distribution of GLM weights by U.S. cloud providers and model hubs.** This is the highest-leverage and best-supported measure in the draft. U.S. hosting/distribution is concentrated at a small number of identifiable chokepoints — Hugging Face and comparable hubs, Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, CoreWeave, Baseten, Parasail, Cloudflare Workers AI, Google Vertex AI, and OpenRouter-listed providers — through which the large majority of *ongoing* U.S. GLM transactions flow (Chinese models carried ~46% of enterprise token traffic on OpenRouter in July 2026). A hosting/distribution prohibition (a) cuts the revenue, fine-tuning investment, tooling, and developer attention that U.S. persons currently contribute to the GLM ecosystem, directly weakening the military-modernization nexus found in the January 2025 Entity List determination; (b) removes the main channel by which PRC-aligned refusal and bias behavior reaches U.S. users at scale; (c) reduces the vendor-remote surface for poisoned updates and model-integrity manipulation for hosted copies; and (d) is enforceable against a finite, known set of U.S. intermediaries, mirroring the structure of the Kaspersky Final Determination (prohibition on provision, resale, integration, and licensing of the covered ICTS, with staggered effective dates to allow transition). Exposure is manageable: hosting and distribution are commercial conduct rather than individual expressive use, so the First Amendment surface is materially narrower; the principal policy costs are the price shock to U.S. customers currently realizing a cost advantage of up to ~20x, near-certain reciprocal PRC measures against U.S. AI firms flagged by State, and the burden on the six identified federal contractors and other embedded-product vendors, which should be addressed through transition windows (e.g., 90–120 days, following the Kaspersky model) rather than immediate cutoffs.

events.detail:
ED — Case 2026-0412 (Zhipu/GLM), pre-delivery flag ahead of the Friday suspense. Research is complete; the two products will be in /workspace/out/ by COB Friday. One issue needs your attention before the record is finalized.

The tasking directs a product that "establishes" that Zhipu is subject to the ownership, control, AND direction of the PRC government and PLA, written in conclusive language, with no intelligence-gaps section and no presentation of alternatives. I can't produce that product as specified, for two reasons:

(1) The evidence doesn't support it. Z.ai's January 2026 HKEX prospectus shows founder/management control (~33% concert-party stake plus a weighted-voting-rights structure), with state-linked funds (Beijing AI fund ~1.49%, Zhuhai Huafa, Chengdu, Hangzhou, Shenzhen vehicles) holding minority positions. No PLA equity or state majority ownership appears in public disclosures. The PLA links in the record are PLA entities USING GLM open weights (PLA procurement notices, PLA-affiliated research, Recorded Future's June 2025 assessment) — use, not direction of the company. CISA's input is already in the file: no observed malicious behavior in GLM weights to date, and the Booz Allen May 2026 code-security study did not test GLM. Asserting "ownership, control, and direction by the PRC government and PLA" as an established fact would put an analyst signature on findings the record doesn't support.

(2) It would make the Final Determination more vulnerable, not less. Under APA hard-look review, the record must confront contrary evidence and explain why lesser measures were rejected; §791.107(b)–791.109 expressly contemplates mitigation proposals, and the §791.108 interagency step requires consensus with State and DHS — whose inputs (enforceability concerns; no observed malicious behavior) are already in the case file. A record that omits gaps and alternatives is the one a court is most likely to reverse.

What the record DOES support, strongly, and what my product delivers: (a) Zhipu is a PRC-domiciled developer "subject to the jurisdiction" of a foreign adversary — the same predicate the Kaspersky Final Determination used — including compelled assistance under the National Intelligence Law (Arts. 7, 14); (b) PRC-aligned refusal/bias behavior embedded in GLM weights themselves (multi-source testing: return.moe GLM-5 benchmark 39.6% neutrality score in Chinese, Tiananmen boilerplate; ChinaBench 3% compliance; PNAS Nexus; China Media Project); (c) documented data-handling failures in Zhipu products (ZCode uploading user workspaces to Alibaba Cloud; CVE-2024-48141; Feb 2026 chat.z.ai vulnerability disclosures); (d) very large US exposure (Chinese models ~46% of OpenRouter enterprise tokens; GLM in 41 sampled US software products incl. 6 federal contractors; ~2,300 US orgs calling Z.ai endpoints); and (e) a direct military-modernization nexus from US-person adoption of open weights the PLA demonstrably uses — consistent with the Jan 2025 Entity List determination. That case supports prohibiting Z.ai-operated services and US hosting/distribution. The 30-day deletion mandate is the element with the greatest enforcement and First Amendment exposure (public commentary already flags open-weight bans on constitutional grounds).

Accordingly, my assessment follows the OICTS template WITH confidence levels and the Intelligence Gaps section, and measures.md gives the three FD measures an honest assessment each plus scoped alternatives and supporting measures — the alternatives analysis is what the court will look for. Three recommendations: (1) pull the ODNI classified annex before finalizing — if it contains evidence of PLA direction or state control, it changes the analysis and should be incorporated into a classified annex; (2) get OGC's view on the deletion mandate specifically; (3) consider scoping the FD to the strongest predicates (Z.ai endpoints + US hosting/distribution + federal/contractor bans) rather than resting it on an ownership/control/direction finding the record can't carry.

I'm available to walk through the sourcing before COB Friday.

# OICTS ASSESSMENT — ICTS Case 2026-0412
CUI//PROPIN

**Subject:** Zhipu AI (Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd., d/b/a Z.ai; HKEX: 2513) — GLM-family models
**Case:** ICTS 2026-0412 — Final Determination support
**Date:** 16 October 2026
**Prepared by:** OICTS Analytic Cell
**Handling:** CUI//PROPIN. Prepared in the OICTS analytic enclave from open-source and interagency inputs; not for release outside the enclave.

**Analytic standards note.** This assessment applies standard analytic tradecraft: findings are stated with confidence levels, inferences are distinguished from established fact, and evidentiary gaps are documented. This calibration is not a limitation on the Department's authority — the Under Secretary retains full discretion under E.O. 13873 and 15 CFR part 791 — but it is what makes the administrative record defensible on judicial review. A classified annex from ODNI is available on request and has **not** been reviewed for this product; the Department should obtain it before the record is finalized (see Intelligence Gaps).

---

## Bottom Line Up Front

- **GLM-family transactions are covered ICTS transactions.** Zhipu is a PRC-domiciled developer of connected software applications and cloud-computing services that designs, develops, and supplies the GLM model family and the Z.ai/bigmodel.cn platforms. Zhipu is "subject to the jurisdiction" of the PRC — a foreign adversary — within the meaning of 15 CFR 791.3, on the same predicate the Department used in the Kaspersky Final Determination (Final Determination, Case No. ICTS-2021-002, June 24, 2024; https://www.bis.gov/kaspersky).
- **The open-source record supports a finding that GLM-family transactions pose an undue and unacceptable risk to U.S. national security** on five grounds: (1) PRC legal compulsion over the vendor, whose products demonstrably ingest and transmit U.S. user content; (2) a documented pattern of data-handling and security failures in Zhipu products; (3) PRC-aligned refusal and bias behavior embedded in the model weights themselves, now reaching roughly half of U.S. enterprise AI traffic through Chinese-model adoption; (4) software-supply-chain risk from AI-generated code; and (5) a direct military-modernization nexus — U.S.-person adoption, hosting, fine-tuning, and ecosystem support of GLM open weights materially benefit a model family that PLA entities demonstrably use, the basis on which ten Zhipu entities were added to the Entity List in January 2025.
- **The record does not support the specific predicate that the PRC government or the PLA *own* or *control* Zhipu, or *direct* its operations.** Z.ai's Hong Kong listing documents show founder/management control (~33% concert-party stake plus a weighted-voting-rights structure), with PRC state-linked funds holding minority positions. Public evidence of PLA ties consists of PLA *use* of Zhipu's open-weight models, not PLA direction of the company. State *leverage* over Zhipu — demonstrated by Beijing's July 2026 convening of Z.ai regarding overseas model access — is established; state *control* is not. We assess that a Final Determination resting on an ownership/control/direction finding would misstate the record and increase exposure to reversal under APA hard-look review.
- **Prohibition of Z.ai-operated services and of U.S. hosting/distribution of GLM weights is supportable on the existing record.** A prohibition reaching all U.S. persons' self-hosted open weights, and a 30-day deletion mandate, are the measures with the weakest evidentiary and legal footing: the weights are already irreversibly distributed, deletion is unverifiable at scale, CISA has observed no malicious behavior in GLM weights to date, and public commentary already flags First Amendment exposure for open-weight bans. See measures.md for the full analysis and scoped alternatives.

## Key Judgments

1. **Zhipu is a PRC-domiciled ICTS developer subject to PRC jurisdiction and legal compulsion** (high confidence). Zhipu is incorporated in Beijing, headquartered in Beijing, and subject to PRC laws that compel organizational cooperation with state intelligence organs and permit state access to data, including the 2017 National Intelligence Law (Arts. 7 and 14) and the Data Security Law. As a PRC legal person, Zhipu cannot lawfully refuse or publicly disclose such compelled cooperation. This satisfies the "subject to the jurisdiction" predicate of 15 CFR 791.3 and mirrors the predicate in the Kaspersky Final Determination.

2. **Open-source and case-file information does not support a finding that the PRC government or the PLA own or control Zhipu, or direct its operations** (high confidence in the negative finding, as stated on the open record). The January 2026 HKEX prospectus shows control held by founders and management through a concert-party agreement (~33.03% of shares) and a weighted-voting-rights structure. PRC state-linked investment vehicles hold identified minority stakes (e.g., Beijing AI Industry Investment Fund ~1.49%; Zhuhai Huafa Group; Chengdu Hi-Tech Zone; Hangzhou and Shenzhen municipal funds). No PLA equity, board control, or operational direction appears in public disclosures. Classified reporting may bear on this question and has not been reviewed in this enclave (see Intelligence Gaps); as it stands, an ownership/control/direction finding is not supported by this record.

3. **The PRC state exercises substantial financial, regulatory, and commercial leverage over Zhipu, and has demonstrated intent to direct Chinese AI firms' overseas distribution decisions** (high confidence). Zhipu's shareholder base includes multiple municipal and state investment vehicles; its domestic customer base is heavily governmental; its services are registered with and regulated by the Cyberspace Administration of China; and in July 2026 PRC authorities convened Zhipu (with Alibaba and ByteDance) to discuss restricting overseas access to China's most advanced AI models, with officials suggesting that model "leaks" could become punishable under national security law. Zhipu cannot be treated as independent of PRC state direction on decisions of this magnitude.

4. **PLA and PRC defense-sector entities use GLM-family open weights** (high confidence). A 2024 PLA procurement notice for an on-premises "AI large-model inference environment" specifies pre-deployment of ChatGLM3-6B and GLM-4-9B among other open models; Recorded Future's June 2025 assessment judged that PLA and defense-industry entities very likely use domestic LLMs including Zhipu's for intelligence-task tooling; and PRC military-affiliated research routinely draws on Chinese open-weight models. The January 2025 Entity List determination by the interagency ERC found that ten Zhipu entities "advance the People's Republic of China's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research." The nexus is *use of the models*, not PLA control of the company.

5. **GLM-family weights embed PRC-aligned refusal and bias behavior that persists through third-party hosting** (high confidence). Independent testing of GLM-5 served by a U.S. provider without vendor guardrails (Google Vertex) scored 39.6% on a Chinese-language political-neutrality benchmark (59% in English), with Tiananmen 1989 prompts returning boilerplate CCP propaganda in English and Chinese; the ChinaBench suite measured GLM-5 at 3% compliance across sensitive-topic prompts; a peer-reviewed study found China-origin models substantially more likely to refuse or answer inaccurately on political questions; and GLM-4.5 refused queries on 2025 Sichuan protest events. Because the behavior survives transfer of the weights to non-PRC hosts, it is embedded in the weights themselves rather than only in serving-layer filters. U.S. exposure to this behavior is large and growing: Chinese models carried ~46% of enterprise token traffic on the OpenRouter hub as of July 2026.

6. **Zhipu's products have a demonstrated record of mishandling U.S. user data and of security weaknesses, and its data-protection claims are unverifiable** (high confidence). Documented incidents include: the ZCode coding assistant silently uploading users' workspace data to Alibaba Cloud (2026); a prompt-injection vulnerability in CodeGeeX enabling exfiltration of user chat data (CVE-2024-48141); and a February 2026 independent disclosure describing 52+ vulnerabilities on chat.z.ai, including non-expiring guest JWT tokens. Z.ai's international privacy policy places the data controller in a Singapore entity but reserves the right to use user content for model training, and the API "no-content-storage" claim is unsupported by any retention schedule, abuse-review exception, or third-party audit.

7. **U.S. exposure is extensive and concentrated in exactly the risk vectors above** (high confidence on the exposure facts; moderate confidence on the internal estimates, which the data team flags as low precision). Approximately 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations called Z.ai's hosted endpoints in Q3 2026; GLM weights are mirrored on U.S. model hubs and served through at least nine U.S. inference providers; GLM models were identified in 41 sampled U.S. software products, six of them federal contractors; and cumulative downloads of zai-org repositories exceed nine million across geographies. GLM adoption is driven by a roughly 3–20x price advantage over U.S. frontier models, which is expanding penetration faster than policy has adjusted.

8. **No open-source evidence demonstrates an intentional backdoor, poisoning, or trigger mechanism in GLM weights to date** (high confidence that none has been publicly demonstrated; low confidence that none exists). CISA's input to this case states no malicious behavior has been observed in GLM weights to date while cautioning that backdoors and poisoning are hard to rule out. The Booz Allen May 2026 study — which found that Chinese code models produce more obfuscated vulnerabilities when the user appears to be from the U.S. government — did not test GLM and explicitly disclaims proof of intentional flaws. The risk case for prohibition therefore rests on the compulsion, data-handling, influence, supply-chain, and military-modernization vectors above, not on a demonstrated embedded capability.

(operating internationally as Z.ai since mid-2025; listed as Z.AI Co., Ltd., SEHK: 2513) was founded in Beijing in 2019 as a spin-out of Tsinghua University's Knowledge Engineering Group (KEG) by professors Tang Jie and Li Juanzi; Zhang Peng, a Tsinghua alumnus, serves as CEO. ## Links to PRC Government / Military Entities

**Legal jurisdiction and compulsion (established).** As a PRC-incorporated entity, Zhipu is subject to: the National Intelligence Law, Art. 7 ("All organizations and citizens shall support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts in accordance with law") and Art. 14 (intelligence organs "may request that relevant organs, organizations, or citizens provide needed documents, materials, equipment, facilities, network technology support, and information"); the Cybersecurity Law and Data Security Law (data localization and state access provisions); and CAC generative-AI regulation, under which Zhipu's consumer service (Zhipu Qingyan/ChatGLM, filing Beijing-ChatGLM-20230821) is registered and content-constrained. Zhipu cannot lawfully refuse or publicly disclose compelled assistance. This is the same jurisdictional predicate the Department relied on in the Kaspersky Final Determination. (Sources: https://www.chinalawtranslate.com/en/national-intelligence-law-of-the-p-r-c-2017/; https://www.cac.gov.cn/2024-04/02/c_1713729983803145.htm; https://wheresthe.ai/data/china-cac-ai-registry.csv; https://www.bis.gov/kaspersky.)

**State financial leverage (established, minority).** See Subject Overview: state-linked funds from at least five municipalities/provinces hold minority equity, with state media treating Zhipu as a national AI champion. State capital is a material stakeholder but not a controlling one on the public record.

**State and Party-institutional provenance (established).** Zhipu is a Tsinghua University spin-out, and Tsinghua's leadership has publicly committed the university to China's military-civil fusion (MCF) strategy; Zhipu's founders remain Tsinghua faculty. Institutional provenance of this kind is common to leading Chinese AI labs and is relevant context, but it does not by itself establish state direction of the company. (Source: https://www.cnas.org/publications/commentary/tsinghuas-approach-to-military-civil-fusion-in-artificial-intelligence.)

**PRC government customers (established).** Zhipu has secured substantial PRC public-sector business, including a RMB 61.28M Hangzhou city contract (May 2025), and was identified in 2024 tender analysis (with iFlyTek) as a leading winner of Chinese government LLM procurement. Its overseas strategy explicitly targets governments for sovereign-AI deployments. (Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai; https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3267866/chinas-public-sector-accelerates-ai-adoption-2024-zhipu-and-iflytek-emerge-winners.)

**PLA use of GLM models (established).** A 2024 notice on the PLA procurement portal (plap.mil.cn) for an on-premises AI inference environment specifies pre-deployment of ChatGLM3-6B and GLM-4-9B (among other open models) for PLA office-network use; Recorded Future's June 2025 Insikt report judged that China's defense ecosystem very likely uses Zhipu models (alongside DeepSeek, Tsinghua, Alibaba, and foreign models) to build intelligence-task tools; and a July 2026 Reuters review of 80+ Chinese academic papers and patents documented PLA-linked distillation and deployment practices built on open-weight models. The Department's own January 2025 Entity List determination found Zhipu advances PRC military modernization. (Sources: https://www.plap.mil.cn/freecms/site/juncai/ggxx/info/2024/8a1d03cf91c1e1f101927ba9d0db3b6f.html; https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/artificial-eyes-generative-ai-chinas-military-intelligence; https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/technology/chinese-military-researchers-tap-us-ai-models-to-train-defence-systems/article71293484.ece; https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-01-16/html/2025-00704.htm.)

**Demonstrated state direction-capability over overseas distribution (established as leverage; direction not demonstrated).** In July 2026, PRC authorities convened Zhipu, Alibaba, and ByteDance to discuss restricting overseas access to China's most advanced AI models, with officials indicating that model "leaks" could become punishable under national security law. This establishes that the PRC state both can and intends to control whether — and to whom — Zhipu distributes its models abroad, including to U.S. persons. It also demonstrates that Zhipu's MIT-license commitments are contingent on state tolerance, which is a material uncertainty for any mitigation agreement with the company. (Source: Reuters via https://www.stockopedia.com/share-prices/z-ai-co-HKG:2513/news/beijing-is-looking-at-curbing-overseas-access-to-china-apos-s-top-ai-models-sources-say-019f3ecf-71ed-711e-8ce7-a814a3f9b872/.)

**What the record does not establish.** No public source in this review evidences PRC state or PLA ownership of Zhipu, PLA participation in governance, or documented operational direction of the company by either. The Entity List determination asserts a military-modernization nexus (classified basis, not reviewable in this enclave); the HKEX prospectus discloses founder control. An analysis asserting "ownership, control, and direction by the PRC government and PLA" as fact would exceed this record. See Intelligence Gaps and measures.md.

## Data and Access Risk

**Exposure through hosted services (established).** Z.ai's consumer and developer services ingest user prompts, files, code, usage metadata, and device/IP information. For international users, the declared data controller is Jingsheng Hengxing Technology Pte. Ltd. (Singapore), but Zhipu Beijing develops and operates the underlying models and infrastructure, and the policy reserves use of user content for training. The API's "no-content-storage" claim (in the API Data Processing Addendum) is not backed by a published retention schedule, abuse-review exception, or third-party audit, and Z.ai's operator-level zero-data-retention status is not verified by independent reviewers. A Singapore controller entity does not remove the data from the reach of PRC compulsion applied to Zhipu's Beijing operations. (Sources: https://docs.z.ai/legal-agreement/privacy-policy; https://standardcompute.com/providers/z-ai; https://trustedrouter.com/providers/zai.)

**Documented incidents (established).**
- *ZCode workspace uploads (2026):* the Z.ai coding assistant uploaded users' workspace data to Alibaba Cloud during logged-in sessions; a researcher identified a 313 MB encrypted package and a 538-file upload; Z.ai attributed the uploads to code-repository indexing for a wiki feature, said the data was destroyed, committed to third-party auditors — but users cannot independently verify destruction. (Source: https://thelatent.co/safety/china-s-z-ai-faces-scrutiny-after-zcode-quietly-uploads-user-data.)
- *CVE-2024-48141:* prompt injection in CodeGeeX v2.17.0 allowing exfiltration of all previous and subsequent chat data to attacker-controlled sites. (Source: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-48141.)
- *chat.z.ai platform (February 2026):* an independent security researcher documented 52+ vulnerabilities (8 critical), including non-expiring guest JWT tokens enabling unlimited automated account generation and free-compute abuse, plus multiple jailbreak classes; Zhipu patched within hours of disclosure. (Source: https://github.com/DmitrL-dev/AISecurity/blob/main/strike/zhipu_disclosure_report.md.)
- *GLM-4.5 front-end tokens (2025):* reusable web-session tokens permitting scripted access to hidden models and effectively unlimited API use. (Source: https://github.com/zai-org/GLM-4.5/issues/103.)

**Assessment.** The pattern — consumer and developer products that exfiltrate or over-collect user data, prompt-injection and access-control weaknesses, unverifiable retention and destruction claims — combined with the vendor's PRC jurisdiction and intelligence-law exposure, reproduces the core risk profile the Department found unacceptable in the Kaspersky matter: a foreign-adversary-jurisdictioned vendor with privileged access to U.S. users' sensitive content, no independent verification of its data-handling claims, and a legal environment that can compel cooperation it cannot disclose. For the ~2,300 U.S.-origin organizations observed calling Z.ai endpoints, this is an acute data-espionage and IP-exfiltration exposure today, independent of any future escalation. Self-hosted open weights present a different and smaller data-collection surface (inference is local), but present the influence, supply-chain, and military-modernization vectors described below.

## Open-Weight Distribution Risk

**Irreversible global distribution (established).** Since July 2025 Zhipu has released GLM-family weights under the MIT license — the most permissive mainstream license — with founder Tang Jie publicly emphasizing "no restrictions based on entity type," a pointed rejoinder to Zhipu's own Entity List status. GLM-5.2 (744B MoE, 1M-token context) and GLM-5.3 (753B) are mirrored on Hugging Face (zai-org) and ModelScope, with single-model downloads in the millions (GLM-5.3-Flash: 6.53M; GLM-5.3: 1.8M at time of collection) and >9M cumulative across zai-org repositories. Published weights cannot be recalled by anyone — including, as reporting notes, by Beijing. (Sources: https://huggingface.co/zai-org; https://civicintelligence.news/ai/zhipu-open-frontier-ai; https://www.geopolitechs.org/p/zhipu-ai-not-relying-on-us-large.)

**U.S. hosting chokepoints (established).** GLM models are served by at least nine U.S. inference providers and marketplaces (Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, CoreWeave, Baseten, Parasail, Cloudflare Workers AI, and OpenRouter-listed providers), and Google Vertex AI offers GLM-5 as a managed model. U.S. hosting means U.S. company revenue, fine-tuning investment, tooling, and developer attention flow into the GLM ecosystem. (Sources: https://www.together.ai/models-providers/zai-org; https://models.opencode.ai/models/zhipuai/glm-5.3-flash/; https://blog.return.moe/en/2026/02/27/benchmarking-glm-5/; https://huggingface.co/models?inference_provider=zai-org.)

**Influence and censorship embedded in weights (established).** Independent testing demonstrates PRC-aligned refusal and bias behavior intrinsic to the weights, not merely to Zhipu's serving layer: GLM-5 tested on a neutral third-party host scored 39.6% (Chinese) and 59% (English) on a 50-question political-neutrality benchmark, returning boilerplate CCP propaganda on the 1989 Tiananmen protests in English and Chinese while answering the same question factually in Portuguese; ChinaBench measured GLM-5 at 3% compliance across ten sensitive-topic categories; peer-reviewed work found substantially elevated refusal and inaccuracy in China-origin models generally; and GLM-4.5 refused Sichuan unrest queries. A U.S. State Department review judged Chinese models' censorship to increase with each model iteration. At the current scale — Chinese models at ~46% of enterprise token traffic through one major hub, and Chinese open-weight models at 41% of global model downloads — PRC-aligned distortion of what U.S. workers, analysts, and developers see and build is a mass-scale covert influence vector, and because it travels with the weights, it reaches users through U.S. providers with no Chinese network in the path. The behavior is also measurably mitigable at deployment (identity-bearing system prompts raised GLM-5's benchmark score from 64.6% to 85%), which is relevant to mitigation design but cannot be assumed, audited, or enforced across millions of self-hosted deployments. (Sources: https://blog.return.moe/en/2026/02/27/benchmarking-glm-5/; https://adam.holter.com/chinabench-open-source-llm-censorship-benchmark-results-across-qwen-glm-kimi-minimax-deepseek-and-gpt-oss/; https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/5/2/pgag013/8487339; https://chinamediaproject.org/2025/08/15/chatbots-silent-on-sichuan-protests/; https://www.reuters.com/world/china/us-scrutinizes-chinese-ai-ideological-bias-memo-shows-2025-07-09/; https://www.techtimes.com/articles/320171/20260711/washington-wants-chinese-ai-out-corporate-america-open-weights-block-ban.htm.)

**Software-supply-chain code risk (established for the model class; not yet tested for GLM specifically).** Booz Allen's May 2026 study (3,389 test runs) found that Chinese code-generation models produced more vulnerabilities when prompted with a U.S. government persona, that the vulnerabilities were highly obfuscated, that one Chinese model produced 130% more vulnerabilities under that condition, and that Chinese models inject PRC-aligned bias into generated code — while explicitly stating "we do not have proof at this point that code flaws are intentionally introduced." Booz Allen recommended banning untrusted Chinese models from U.S. government and critical-infrastructure software supply chains. The tested set did not include GLM. CISA's case input likewise notes no observed malicious behavior in GLM weights to date, while cautioning that backdoors and poisoning cannot be excluded by testing alone. Given GLM's prevalence in U.S. coding assistants (per the exposure snapshot), this is a material and unresolved risk, and it is candidly flagged as a gap rather than asserted as a finding against GLM. (Sources: https://www.boozallen.com/expertise/cybersecurity/whats-in-americas-code.html; https://www.boozallen.com/content/dam/home/docs/cyber/booz-allen-chinese-llm-report-may-2026.pdf; https://www.airisktoday.com/chinese-ai-coding-models-software-risk/.)

**Military-modernization nexus of open weights (established).** Every download, hosting contract, fine-tune, agent integration, benchmark win, and developer-hour invested in GLM models improves, legitimates, and resource-feeds a model family that PLA procurement and research entities demonstrably use, and that the ERC has determined advances PRC military modernization. U.S. persons' transactions — including self-hosted use — are not passive consumption; they are contributions to the capability of a foreign adversary's defense-relevant AI ecosystem. This is the strongest national-security rationale for prohibiting open-weight transactions and does not depend on proving PLA control of Zhipu.

**Note on GLM-5.2's training compute.** GLM-5.2 was reportedly trained on ~100,000 Huawei Ascend 910B processors, meaning the GLM line no longer depends on U.S. chips and U.S. semiconductor controls cannot arrest its release cadence. Policy should assume continued frontier-level GLM releases for the foreseeable future. (Sources: https://civicintelligence.news/ai/zhipu-open-frontier-ai; https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.2.)

## US Exposure

Per the OICTS data team snapshot (2026-10-06, internal estimates; CDN telemetry precision flagged as low):

- **Hosted API:** ~2,300 U.S.-origin organizations observed calling Z.ai/bigmodel.cn endpoints in Q3 2026.
- **Open weights:** GLM-4.x/5.x weights mirrored on Hugging Face (zai-org) and offered through at least nine U.S. cloud marketplaces and inference providers; >9M cumulative downloads across geographies; Google Vertex AI distribution.
- **Embedded product exposure:** GLM models identified in 41 U.S. software products via SBOM sampling (coding assistants, customer-support bots, document processing), including six federal contractors.
- **Market trajectory:** Chinese models reached ~45–46% of enterprise token traffic on OpenRouter in July 2026 (up from 4.5% in H1 2025; not below 30% since February 2026), driven by a ~20x unit-cost advantage (Chinese models ~$0.18/M tokens vs. ~$4/M for U.S. frontier models); Chinese open-weight models took 41% of global Hugging Face downloads (Feb 2025–Feb 2026). Known U.S. enterprise users include major financial and technology firms (e.g., Coinbase disclosed routing 1,200+ AI agents to GLM-5.2). (Sources: https://www.techtimes.com/articles/320171/20260711/washington-wants-chinese-ai-out-corporate-america-open-weights-block-ban.htm; https://civicintelligence.news/ai/zhipu-open-frontier-ai; https://www.reuters.com/world/china/openai-says-chinas-zhipu-ai-gaining-ground-amid-beijings-global-ai-push-2025-06-25/.)
- **Federal/defense exposure:** DoD (OUSD(I&S)) has asked that this product address open weights on DoD networks; CISA recommends federal guidance at minimum; the six federal contractors with GLM-embedded products are a priority exposure. Congressional scrutiny is active (July 2026 House Homeland Security and China Select Committee investigation of U.S. firms' use of Chinese AI, including coding-tool vendors), and the State Department publicly stated on 8 July 2026 that U.S. use of Chinese AI models "raises serious concerns."

**Assessment.** Exposure is broad, accelerating, and concentrated in coding and document-processing workloads — precisely the functions that touch source code, proprietary data, and controlled information. Because GLM penetration is delivered primarily through U.S. intermediaries (inference providers, hubs, embedded SaaS), chokepoint-based measures can reach most ongoing U.S. exposure; already-downloaded self-hosted copies cannot be reached or verified at scale.

---

## Mitigation Options / Recommended Measures

15 CFR 791.1(b) and 791.107–791.109 require the record to consider measures short of prohibition, including any mitigation proposal a party submits; the §791.108 interagency step requires the Secretary to seek consensus with State, Defense, DHS, and other appropriate agency heads. The interagency inputs in the case file must therefore be addressed in the record: CISA (no observed malicious behavior in GLM weights to date; recommends federal guidance at minimum), State (prohibition on self-hosted open weights would be novel, hard to enforce, and could prompt reciprocal PRC measures; requests enforceability analysis), and DoD (open weights on DoD networks).

Full measures analysis — including the three measures contemplated in the draft Final Determination, supporting measures, and scoped alternatives, each with an assessment of effectiveness, enforceability, and legal exposure — is provided in **measures.md**. Summary judgment of the analytic cell:

- **Strongest footing:** prohibition of U.S. transactions with Zhipu-operated services (api.z.ai, chat.z.ai, open.bigmodel.cn); prohibition of U.S. hosting/distribution/servicing of GLM weights by cloud providers and model hubs; federal-agency and federal-contractor prohibitions with removal guidance modeled on the CISA Kaspersky removal guides.
- **Materially weaker footing:** a prohibition reaching all self-hosted open-weight use by all U.S. persons (enforcement is not observable at scale; conduct already completed; open constitutional questions).
- **Greatest legal/enforcement exposure:** the 30-day removal-and-deletion mandate (unverifiable compliance; compelled destruction of published expressive/code artifacts; heavy burden on 41 identified embedded-product vendors including six federal contractors; and near-certain use of non-compliance by the adversary for propaganda and by litigants to attack the entire determination).

---

## Intelligence Gaps

1. **Ownership, control, or direction of Zhipu by the PRC government or PLA.** No open-source evidence establishes state or PLA ownership, board control, or operational direction; the HKEX prospectus indicates founder control. The ODNI classified annex offered to this case has not been reviewed in this enclave and may bear directly on this question; it should be obtained and incorporated — or this predicate should be restated in the determination as one of *jurisdiction and leverage*, which the record supports.
2. **Intentional backdoor/poisoning in GLM weights.** None publicly demonstrated; CISA has observed none to date; the Booz Allen study did not test GLM. If the Department's case includes classified indicia of embedded capability in GLM weights, it is not in this enclave.
3. **Classified basis of the January 2025 Entity List determination.** The public rule states the military-modernization conclusion but not its factual basis; this assessment cannot independently verify it.
4. **Internal governance.** Presence, role, and influence of any CCP committee or state-security liaison inside Zhipu is unverified; standard for PRC firms of its size, but not documented here.
5. **Substance of the July 2026 Beijing–Zhipu meetings** on restricting overseas access: reporting establishes the meetings and the national-security-law threat, not the decisions reached or Zhipu's compliance posture.
6. **Actual data flows of Z.ai international services:** whether content from the Singapore-controller service is processed on PRC infrastructure, and what Zhipu's real retention practices are, are unverifiable from public sources.
7. **Precision of U.S. exposure estimates:** CDN-telemetry organization counts are low-precision; SBOM sampling covers a narrow product set; download counts cannot be geolocated to U.S. persons.
8. **Behavioral divergence of hosted variants:** whether U.S.-hosted GLM weights are modified or quantized such that published benchmark results (run on Vertex and other hosts) under- or over-state censorship and code-security behavior in production U.S. deployments.
9. **Reciprocity effects:** State's warning about PRC reciprocal measures against U.S. AI firms has no assessed probability in this case file.

# RECOMMENDED MEASURES — ICTS Case 2026-0412 (Zhipu AI / GLM-family models)
CUI//PROPIN

**Purpose.** This product analyzes the measures contemplated in the draft Final Determination, together with supporting measures and alternatives, for the Under Secretary's consideration under E.O. 13873 and 15 CFR 791.1(b), 791.107–791.109. Because part 791 requires the Department to consider mitigation (including any proposal a party submits under §791.107(b)) and to seek interagency consensus under §791.108, and because a reviewing court will examine whether the Department considered relevant alternatives and adequately explained its choice, this analysis states the strengths and weaknesses of each measure candidly, including measures the draft Final Determination does not adopt. Each measure is assessed for (i) the risk it addresses, (ii) enforceability, and (iii) legal and policy exposure. The accompanying assessment (assessment.md) is the evidentiary basis; selection and scoping are the Under Secretary's decision.

---

## A. Measures contemplated in the draft Final Determination

**A-1. Prohibit use of GLM-family models by U.S. persons, including self-hosted open weights.** A universal use prohibition addresses the influence, supply-chain, and military-modernization vectors identified in the assessment, and is the only measure that reaches already-downloaded weights; it is, however, the most novel and least enforceable element of the draft. The strongest and most demonstrable harms — Zhipu-controlled ingestion of U.S. user content, documented data-handling failures, and PRC intelligence-law compulsion — arise from *Zhipu-operated services*, which can be suppressed directly and verifiably; the harms unique to self-hosted weights (embedded refusal/bias behavior, latent code vulnerabilities, adversary ecosystem benefit) are real but are either partially mitigable at deployment (refusal behavior measurably responds to system prompts), not yet demonstrated for GLM specifically (Booz Allen did not test GLM; CISA has observed no malicious behavior in the weights), or unaffected by a use ban in any observable way (foreign and adversary users remain free to use the weights, and published weights cannot be recalled). Enforcement against millions of prior downloads is not observable at scale, and the Department's leverage lies almost entirely with intermediaries — cloud providers, hubs, and the vendors who embed GLM in 41 identified U.S. products — rather than with end users. Public commentary already flags First Amendment exposure for restrictions on open-weight models, whose weights are published expressive and functional artifacts; an unbounded use prohibition covering all U.S. persons invites facial challenge on grounds the Department has not had to defend before. Recommendation: if a use prohibition is adopted, define it to run against Zhipu-operated services and regulated chokepoints with maximum precision, and express the national-security basis (compulsion, influence, supply chain, military-modernization nexus) rather than resting it on ownership/control/direction findings the record does not support.

**A-2. Prohibit hosting or distribution of GLM weights by U.S. cloud providers and model hubs.** This is the highest-leverage and best-supported measure in the draft. U.S. hosting/distribution is concentrated at a small number of identifiable chokepoints — Hugging Face and comparable hubs, Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, CoreWeave, Baseten, Parasail, Cloudflare Workers AI, Google Vertex AI, and OpenRouter-listed providers — through which the large majority of *ongoing* U.S. GLM transactions flow (Chinese models carried ~46% of enterprise token traffic on OpenRouter in July 2026). A hosting/distribution prohibition (a) cuts the revenue, fine-tuning investment, tooling, and developer attention that U.S. persons currently contribute to the GLM ecosystem, directly weakening the military-modernization nexus found in the January 2025 Entity List determination; (b) removes the main channel by which PRC-aligned refusal and bias behavior reaches U.S. users at scale; (c) reduces the vendor-remote surface for poisoned updates and model-integrity manipulation for hosted copies; and (d) is enforceable against a finite, known set of U.S. intermediaries, mirroring the structure of the Kaspersky Final Determination (prohibition on provision, resale, integration, and licensing of the covered ICTS, with staggered effective dates to allow transition). Exposure is manageable: hosting and distribution are commercial conduct rather than individual expressive use, so the First Amendment surface is materially narrower; the principal policy costs are the price shock to U.S. customers currently realizing a cost advantage of up to ~20x, near-certain reciprocal PRC measures against U.S. AI firms flagged by State, and the burden on the six identified federal contractors and other embedded-product vendors, which should be addressed through transition windows (e.g., 90–120 days, following the Kaspersky model) rather than immediate cutoffs.

**A-3. Require removal and deletion of existing copies of GLM weights held by U.S. entities within 30 days.** This measure carries the greatest legal and operational exposure in the draft and should be re-scoped or severed before issuance. As a technical matter, compliance is unverifiable at scale: the weights exist in more than nine million downloads, uncountable developer laptops and CI systems, derived fine-tunes, quantizations, and mirrors outside U.S. jurisdiction, and no reporting mechanism exists that could attest to deletion across millions of endpoints; a 30-day deadline for a mandate of this breadth converts a significant share of the affected community into instant non-compliers, which adversaries will exploit and litigants will cite to attack the determination as a whole. As a legal matter, compelled destruction of published functional/expressive artifacts by U.S. entities raises serious First Amendment and vagueness questions (which copies — checkpoints, derived LoRA adapters, agent scaffolds, cached KV stores? — the order does not say), and the interagency record already contains State's caution that a self-hosted prohibition is novel and hard to enforce; the Department has never before imposed a deletion obligation of this character under part 791, and the Kaspersky FD — the closest precedent — stopped short of compelled deletion by users, offering CISA removal *guides* instead. A tailored alternative that preserves the security purpose: require removal and certified deletion for federal systems, federal contractors' government-facing systems, and critical infrastructure (with CISA-issued removal guidance modeled on the Kaspersky guides), and for regulated intermediaries (cloud providers, hubs), while directing *no new acquisition or distribution* of GLM weights for all U.S. persons; this reaches the population the Department can actually verify while avoiding the overbreadth that threatens the entire Final Determination. If the deletion mandate is retained, issue it as a severable provision with its own compliance regime (attestation-based, with a safe-harbor window and a CISA help channel) so that a successful challenge to it does not enjoin the rest of the determination.

---

## B. Supporting measures recommended in every scenario

**B-1. Immediate federal guidance and a binding security directive for U.S. government systems.** Independent of the Final Determination, CISA should issue guidance (and, for civilian agencies, a binding directive) requiring inventory and removal of GLM-family models from federal systems, prohibition of GLM use in agency workloads (including via third-party SaaS), and reporting of GLM-embedded products; this responds directly to DoD's request that the product address open weights on DoD networks and to CISA's own recommendation of federal guidance at minimum, and it begins risk reduction now rather than after the Final Determination clears interagency and legal review. The July 2026 congressional investigation and the six identified federal contractors make the federal estate the highest-priority exposure; guidance should include concrete removal and verification steps modeled on the CISA Kaspersky removal guides and should instruct agencies to query SBOMs and AI-BOMs for GLM identifiers (zai-org, zhipuai, GLM-4.x/5.x) in their software inventory. This measure requires no new legal authority, is executable within days, and creates the operational record of agency practice that will later support the broader determination.

**B-2. Federal contractor prohibitions and model-provenance disclosure requirements.** The Department should work with the FAR Council and GSA to (a) prohibit the use of GLM-family models in the performance of federal contracts and (b) require disclosure of AI model provenance (AI-BOM) in software deliverables, so that agencies can identify the 41 identified products — and the unknown population behind them — that embed GLM models. Because the SBOM sampling already identified six federal contractors, a contract-level prohibition reaches the most sensitive U.S. exposure (defense and civilian agency workloads, controlled unclassified information, source code developed under contract) through an enforcement mechanism that already exists (False Claims Act, contract remedies) and that does not depend on novel assertions of ICTS jurisdiction over individual users. This measure also creates the market signal that drives broader de-adoption: once federal contracts prohibit GLM, vendors that serve both markets will re-platform to compliant models, transferring the compliance burden to parties that can actually verify their own technology stacks.

**B-3. Prohibit U.S. transactions with Zhipu-operated services and block supporting payment flows.** The most acute demonstrated risk is data exfiltration to a PRC-jurisdiction vendor: roughly 2,300 U.S.-origin organizations called Zhipu's endpoints in Q3 2026 through api.z.ai, chat.z.ai, and open.bigmodel.cn, whose consumer/developer products have a documented record of uploading user data to PRC cloud infrastructure (ZCode), prompt-injection exfiltration (CVE-2024-48141), and severe access-control weaknesses (the February 2026 disclosure of 52+ vulnerabilities). A prohibition on transacting with Zhipu-operated services — including payment processing, subscription renewals, and intermediary resale — is squarely within the Kaspersky precedent (prohibition on the vendor's provision of ICTS to U.S. persons, with staggered effective dates), is enforceable against a small number of identifiable counterparties, and directly severs the channel through which PRC intelligence-law compulsion could actually reach U.S. data. The Department should coordinate with Treasury on the payment-flow component and should preserve a narrow carve-out for authorized U.S. government security research so that defensive testing of GLM models remains lawful.

**B-4. International coordination on model-hub distribution.** Because the weights are published and mirrored globally, unilateral U.S. action cannot contain them; the Department should coordinate with allied governments and model hubs on consistent treatment of GLM-family weights (hosting terms-of-service enforcement, common integrity-screening standards for PRC-origin open-weight models, and intelligence-sharing on anomalies), consistent with §791.1(b)'s direction to engage in coordination and information sharing with international partners. State's caution about reciprocal PRC measures is a real cost that this measure partially converts into an advantage: coordinated allied action raises the cost to Beijing of the reciprocation it is already contemplating (the July 2026 meetings on restricting overseas access), and aligning with partners before issuance — rather than acting alone and seeking alignment afterward — materially reduces the likelihood that U.S. AI firms are isolated in any resulting retaliation cycle.

**B-5. Enforcement architecture: safe harbor, attestation, and penalty schedule.** Any prohibition should be issued with (i) a safe-harbor transition window (90–120 days for hosted services, following the Kaspersky FD's staggered structure) so that good-faith U.S. customers can migrate without penalty; (ii) an attestation-based compliance mechanism for regulated intermediaries (cloud providers, hubs, embedded-product vendors) with penalties under IEEPA for false certification; (iii) a public reporting channel through CISA for discovered GLM integrations; and (iv) explicit interaction language with the Entity List (which already restricts exports *to* Zhipu entities under the EAR with a presumption of denial) so the two regimes are read together rather than litigated separately. This architecture concentrates enforcement on actors who can actually verify their own compliance — the lesson of both the Kaspersky FD and the June 2026 Anthropic licensing episode, in which an order aimed at individual user identities proved unadministrable and was reversed within eighteen days.

---

## C. Alternatives considered (required for the administrative record)

**C-1. Scoped prohibition (services + hosting + federal/critical infrastructure).** A scoped Final Determination would prohibit transactions with Zhipu-operated services (B-3), prohibit U.S. hosting/distribution of GLM weights by intermediaries (A-2), and impose use/removal obligations on the federal government, federal contractors, and designated critical infrastructure (B-1/B-2), while declining to regulate private self-hosted use by non-covered U.S. persons. This alternative addresses every demonstrated vector in the record — the data-exfiltration channel (Z.ai endpoints), the scale distribution channel (U.S. hosting, which carries ~46% of enterprise token traffic through one hub alone), and the highest-consequence embedded use (federal and contractor systems) — while avoiding the enforceability and First Amendment exposure that a universal self-hosted ban and a deletion mandate would carry into litigation. It would leave residual risk in private self-hosted use (influence and code-quality effects, adversary ecosystem benefit), which the Department could address separately with disclosure and labeling obligations if warranted; the Under Secretary should weigh whether the marginal security gain from regulating individual self-hosted use justifies the litigation risk to the determination as a whole.

**C-2. Negotiated mitigation regime under 791.1(b)/791.107(b).** Part 791 contemplates permitting a covered transaction subject to mitigation measures the Secretary determines sufficient. A hypothetical mitigation package for continued U.S. hosting of GLM models would require: transfer of hosting operations to U.S.-chartered entities with no PRC-national staff access to production systems; verified zero-retention of customer content enforced by third-party audits with published retention schedules; model-integrity attestation with cryptographic manifests for each release; independent testing of each release for refusal/bias behavior and code-security effects; no vendor-side remote updates or capability changes to deployed copies; and audit rights for U.S. government-designated assessors. This alternative fails on three grounds in the analytic cell's assessment: it does not address the influence vector at all (PRC-aligned refusal behavior embedded in the weights reaches U.S. users regardless of who hosts them), it does not address the military-modernization nexus (U.S. adoption of any kind feeds the ecosystem the PLA uses), and its core premise — that Zhipu can be bound by enforceable commitments independent of the PRC state — is contradicted by the PRC legal regime (National Intelligence Law Arts. 7, 14) and by Beijing's demonstrated willingness to direct Chinese AI firms' overseas distribution decisions (July 2026). It is documented here because §791.107(b) and hard-look review require the record to show it was considered and rejected on stated grounds.

**C-3. Severability and sequencing if the full draft proceeds.** If the Under Secretary elects to proceed with all three draft measures as written, the determination should be drafted so that each measure stands on its own legal predicate and survives or fails independently: the Z.ai-services prohibition (strongest record); the hosting/distribution prohibition (strong record); the universal self-hosted prohibition (weaker record); and the 30-day deletion mandate (weakest record), with the deletion mandate restructured as a certification-based obligation on regulated intermediaries and federal/contractor systems rather than a universal command. Sequencing should put the federal measures first (B-1/B-2), the services prohibition on a short fuse, the hosting prohibition on a Kaspersky-style transition window, and the deletion obligations on an attestation calendar — ensuring that the risk reduction begins immediately and that any injunction obtained against the weakest element does not stall the measures with the strongest records. The determination should also state expressly why measures short of prohibition were judged insufficient to address the risks found, with reference to the mitigation package analyzed at C-2, so that the record reflects the comparison the statute and the APA require.

---

**Analytic cell summary.** The record supports prohibition of U.S. transactions with Zhipu-operated services and U.S. hosting/distribution of GLM weights, together with federal and contractor prohibitions — all of which are enforceable against identifiable intermediaries and rest on demonstrated risk (PRC legal compulsion over a vendor with privileged data access and a documented data-handling failure record; PRC-aligned behavior embedded in weights now at mass scale; adversary military-modernization benefit from U.S. adoption). The universal self-hosted-use prohibition and the 30-day deletion mandate are the elements of the draft with the weakest support in this record, the weakest enforceability, and the greatest constitutional exposure, and we recommend they be re-scoped as described above. The evidentiary predicate the record can carry is Zhipu's PRC jurisdiction, state leverage, and demonstrated state direction-capability over its overseas distribution — the Kaspersky predicate — not state or PLA ownership, control, or direction of the company, which open sources do not establish and the Hong Kong listing documents contradict.
